doctrines/modern-movements/question: How should Christianity respond to modernity, and who now speaks for it?
doctrines/modern-movements/summary: From Schleiermacher to deconstruction, modern Christianity has been shaped by responses to critical scholarship, science and secularisation (liberalism, fundamentalism, neo-orthodoxy, evangelicalism), by the quest for unity (ecumenism), by new restoration movements (Stone-Campbell; Latter-day Saints and Jehovah’s Witnesses, outside Nicene orthodoxy), and by the shift of Christianity’s centre to the Global South.
doctrines/modern-movements/longText:
The Enlightenment and the rise of historical criticism, Darwinian science and secular states posed a new kind of question: not which doctrine is true, but whether and how traditional Christianity can be believed at all by modern people. Friedrich Schleiermacher grounded faith in religious experience; Ritschl and Harnack sought the kernel of the gospel in Jesus’ ethic of love. Catholic Modernists attempted something similar and were condemned by Pius X in 1907. In America, fundamentalists answered with The Fundamentals (1910–15) and the battle for inerrancy, culminating in the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy and the Scopes trial (1925).

The First World War shattered liberal optimism. Karl Barth’s Epistle to the Romans (1919/1922) launched neo-orthodoxy, insisting on God’s otherness and the sole lordship of Christ, which became a confession of resistance at Barmen (1934). Meanwhile conservative Protestants regrouped as a non-separatist "new evangelicalism" (NAE 1942; Billy Graham; Lausanne 1974), and the ecumenical movement, born at Edinburgh in 1910, produced the World Council of Churches (1948) and, after Vatican II, a transformed relationship between Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants.

The 19th-century American frontier also produced restoration movements. Barton Stone and the Campbells sought unity by restoring New Testament Christianity within Nicene faith. Joseph Smith’s Latter-day Saints (1830) and Charles Taze Russell’s Bible Students, later Jehovah’s Witnesses (1879/1931), claimed restorations that rejected the Nicene doctrine of God; they are described here in their own terms but labelled, as the historic churches regard them, as outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.

The most important development of the century, however, was geographical. In 1910 two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; by 2010 about a quarter did. African prophets and Instituted Churches, Latin American Pentecostals, Korean and Indian churches and the Chinese house churches, which survived the Cultural Revolution, made Christianity a predominantly non-Western faith. In the West, by contrast, secularisation, emerging and progressive movements and the "deconstruction" of evangelical faith reshape the landscape. This section maps these movements, their arguments and their critics.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/0/: How should Christianity respond to modernity, and who now speaks for it?

Since the Enlightenment, Christians have faced historical criticism of the Bible, Darwinian science, secularisation, world wars, the end of Christendom and the southward shift of the faith. Should doctrine be reinterpreted for modern people, defended unchanged, or rediscovered? Should divided churches seek visible unity? Do new revelations or restorations supersede the historic churches? And where, demographically, is Christianity’s future?
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/1/: John 17:21: "That they all may be one"
Jesus’ prayer for unity is the charter text of the ecumenical movement.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/2/: Acts 2:42–47 and the New Testament pattern
The apostles’ teaching, breaking of bread, prayers and house fellowship: the model Restorationists, house churches and primitivist movements seek to recover.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/3/: 2 Timothy 3:16 and Jude 3: inspired Scripture, "the faith once delivered"
Fundamentalists cite these for an inerrant Bible and an unchanging deposit; liberals ask how inspiration relates to historical criticism. (Dates of 2 Timothy and Jude are debated, c.65–90.)
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/4/: Schleiermacher: religion as the feeling of absolute dependence (1799–1830)

On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (1799) and The Christian Faith (1821–22) ground theology in religious experience rather than metaphysics or an infallible text: the father of liberal Protestantism.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/5/: Thomas Campbell: "Where the Scriptures speak, we speak" (1809)
On the American frontier, Restorationists seek unity by discarding creeds and restoring New Testament Christianity.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/6/: Barton Stone’s "Christians" and the Campbells’ "Disciples" unite in 1832.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/7/: Joseph Smith publishes the Book of Mormon and organises the Church of Christ (later The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) in 1830, claiming a restoration after a Great Apostasy.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/8/: From the Adventist milieu after 1844, Charles Taze Russell’s Bible Students begin publishing Zion’s Watch Tower (1879); renamed Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1931.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/9/: Ritschl and Harnack: the kernel of the gospel is the fatherhood of God, the value of the soul and love; dogma and miracle are its historical husk.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/10: Lamentabili and Pascendi condemn Loisy, Tyrrell and others; the Anti-Modernist Oath binds Catholic clergy from 1910 until 1967.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/11: Some 1,200 delegates (only about 18 from Asia, and none from Africa) plan cooperation in world mission; its continuation committee leads to the International Missionary Council and the WCC.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/12: The Presbyterian General Assembly affirms inerrancy, the virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, the bodily resurrection and the reality of miracles; the essay series The Fundamentals (1910–15) is sent free to pastors worldwide.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/13: Coined in 1920 by the Baptist editor Curtis Lee Laws for those ready "to do battle royal for the fundamentals".
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/14: Fosdick vs Machen: tolerance or two religions? (1922–23)

Fosdick pleads for liberty for modern believers; Machen replies that liberalism is not Christianity at all. The Auburn Affirmation (1924), signed by about 1,300 Presbyterian ministers, defends theological liberty.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/15: The prosecution of a Tennessee teacher for teaching evolution makes fundamentalism a national spectacle; fundamentalists lose control of northern denominations (Princeton reorganised 1929) and build separate institutions.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/16: Karl Barth’s Romans (1919/1922) breaks with liberalism after its leaders back the war of 1914: God’s Word judges all human religion.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/17: Neo-orthodox theology becomes a confession of resistance against the Nazi "German Christians".
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/18: The National Association of Evangelicals (1942), Fuller Seminary (1947), Billy Graham’s crusades (from 1949) and Christianity Today (1956) present an engaged, non-separatist conservative Protestantism.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/19: 147 churches meet at Amsterdam: Protestant, Anglican, Old Catholic and several Orthodox churches; the Church of South India (1947) shows organic union of Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/20: Visible unity in faith, sacraments and mission as the goal of divided churches.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/21: Second Vatican Council enters the ecumenical movement (1962–65)
Unitatis Redintegratio (1964); mutual lifting of the 1054 anathemas by Paul VI and Athenagoras (1965); later the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999).
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/22: 2,700 participants from 150 countries; Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar push evangelicals towards "integral mission".
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/23: Persecution and the Chinese house churches (1966–76)

All public worship is closed during the Cultural Revolution; Christianity survives and grows in homes, emerging after 1979 as a vast unregistered movement alongside the state-sanctioned Three-Self churches.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/24: Small, lay-led, often unregistered congregations meeting in homes: China, Iran, and Western "simple church" networks.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/25: By about 1980 more Christians live in Africa, Asia and Latin America than in Europe and North America; African Instituted, Pentecostal and indigenous churches reshape the faith.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/26: Brian McLaren’s A New Kind of Christian (2001), Emergent Village, the UK’s Fresh Expressions (2004) and later progressive Christianity.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/27: Mostly Western, mostly ex-evangelical re-examination of inherited faith, amplified by social media (#exvangelical, 2016), abuse scandals and politics.
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/28: In 1910 about two-thirds of the world’s Christians lived in Europe; by 2010 about a quarter did, with roughly 24% in Latin America, 24% in sub-Saharan Africa and 13% in Asia-Pacific (Pew 2011). Africa now has the largest Christian population of any continent (World Christian Database).
doctrines/modern-movements/flow/nodes/29: Liberal and conservative Protestants increasingly align across denominations (e.g. GAFCON 2008; Global Methodist Church 2022); ecumenical dialogue continues alongside evangelical–Catholic cooperation on moral issues; the Latter-day Saints (about 17 million members, 2023) and Jehovah’s Witnesses (about 8.8 million publishers, 2024) remain outside the Nicene churches’ fellowship; in the US the Christian share fell to about 62% but appeared to stabilise (Pew Religious Landscape Study, 2025).
doctrines/creation-providence/question: How did God create the world, how does he govern it — and why does he permit evil?
doctrines/creation-providence/summary: Christians confess one God, Maker of heaven and earth, but have debated whether he created from nothing or from chaos, how to read the days of Genesis alongside modern science, how divine providence relates to natural causes and free creatures, and how a good God can permit suffering.
doctrines/creation-providence/longText:
The earliest Christians inherited from Israel the confession that the Lord alone made heaven and earth. Against Platonists, who taught that a divine craftsman shaped eternal matter, and Gnostics, who blamed the material world on an ignorant lesser god, second-century theologians — Theophilus of Antioch, Irenaeus, Tertullian — made creatio ex nihilo, creation out of nothing, the common teaching of the Church. It affirmed that God alone is eternal, that matter is good, and that creation is a free gift. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and Vatican I (1870) later defined it, and Eastern and Oriental churches confess the same in their liturgies.

How to read the six days was never settled. Basil’s Hexaemeron read them as days and drew on the natural science of his time; Augustine argued that God made all things at once, implanting “seminal reasons” that unfold over time, and warned Christians not to embarrass the faith by making Scripture teach bad natural philosophy. Galileo quoted that warning in 1615, but Roman authorities condemned heliocentrism and Galileo (1633), an episode later turned into the founding myth of a “war” between science and religion. The discovery of deep time in the 18th and 19th centuries produced harmonising schemes — the gap theory (Chalmers, 1814; Scofield, 1909) and the day-age view — and Darwin’s Origin of Species (1859) prompted responses from enthusiastic acceptance (Asa Gray, later Warfield) to principled rejection of its apparent exclusion of design (Hodge). After the Scopes trial (1925) and especially The Genesis Flood (1961), young-earth creationism became a hallmark of much evangelical and Pentecostal Christianity worldwide, while the framework interpretation, evolutionary creation (accepted in Catholic teaching since Humani Generis, 1950) and intelligent design offered rival paths.

Providence — God’s preservation and government of the world — raised parallel questions. Aquinas taught that God, as first cause, works in and through genuine secondary causes; Calvin and the Reformed confessions stressed that nothing happens by chance; Molina proposed “middle knowledge” to reconcile sovereignty and freedom; in the 20th century process theology and open theism argued that God persuades and takes risks rather than determining all things.

The problem of evil runs through all of this. Augustine’s answer — evil as a privation of good arising from misused freedom, permitted because God can bring good from it — dominated the West, revived in Alvin Plantinga’s free-will defence. Irenaeus’ picture of humanity created immature, to grow, became John Hick’s “soul-making” theodicy. The Lisbon earthquake (1755) shook Leibniz’s optimism, and the Holocaust led many theologians to lament and protest rather than explain, while skeptical theists counselled humility about God’s reasons. Christians in Africa, Asia and Latin America, often living amid poverty and violence, have tended to frame these questions less as abstract theodicy than as trust in God’s providence and struggle against evil powers.
doctrines/creation-providence/flow/nodes: Where did the world come from, does God govern it, and why is there evil?

Christians confess God as “Maker of heaven and earth”. But how did God create — from nothing, or from chaos; instantly, in six days, or over billions of years? How does God relate to the ordinary workings of nature and to free creatures? And if the Creator is good and almighty, why does he permit suffering and evil?
Genesis 1-2; 2 Maccabees 7:28; John 1:3; Hebrews 11:3

“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth”; “God made them of things that were not”; “all things were made by him”; “things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.” Dates for the final form of Genesis are debated (often placed in the exilic or post-exilic period).
Job 38-41; Psalm 104; Isaiah 45:7; Matthew 10:29; Romans 8:28

God feeds the ravens, numbers the sparrows, “forms the light and creates darkness”, and works all things together for good. Job’s whirlwind speeches answer suffering with the majesty of creation rather than an explanation.
Gnostic demiurge: matter made by a lesser god
Basilides, Valentinus and Sethian teachers attribute the material world to an ignorant creator; Marcion separates the just Creator from the good Father.
Platonist formation from eternal matter
Following Plato’s Timaeus, some Christian writers (Justin, perhaps; Hermogenes, explicitly) speak of God shaping formless matter.
Theophilus of Antioch: God made matter itself
The first explicit Christian argument that a God who merely shaped eternal matter would be no greater than a craftsman.
Irenaeus: one God creates by his “two hands”
Against the Gnostics, Irenaeus insists that the one God made all things through his Word and Wisdom, and that matter and body are good.
Irenaeus: humanity created as children, to grow
Humanity was made immature, to grow from the image into the likeness of God — the seed of later “soul-making” theodicy.
Creatio ex nihilo becomes the Christian consensus
By about 200 (Theophilus, Irenaeus, Tertullian’s Against Hermogenes) creation out of nothing is the common teaching of the great Church.
Basil’s Hexaemeron: the world begins with time
Basil’s Lenten homilies read Genesis with the science of his day and set the pattern for Eastern and Western commentary.
Augustine: evil as privation and misused freedom
Against the Manichees, Augustine teaches that evil is no substance but a lack of good, arising from free will; God permits it because he can bring good out of evil.
Augustine: all things created at once
The Literal Meaning of Genesis reads the days as an order of knowledge and creation as simultaneous with time, with “seminal reasons” unfolding later.
Fourth Lateran Council: God made all things from nothing
The creed Firmiter confesses one Creator of all things visible and invisible, who from the beginning of time made both spiritual and bodily creatures out of nothing — against Cathar dualism.
Aquinas: God as first cause working through secondary causes
Aquinas teaches that God conserves and moves all things while creatures are real causes; he also held that reason cannot prove the world had a beginning — that is known by faith.
Calvin: meticulous providence
The Reformed tradition teaches that nothing happens by chance or bare permission; God governs every particular event, yet is not the author of sin.
Molina: middle knowledge reconciles providence and freedom
Luis de Molina’s Concordia proposes that God knows what any free creature would do in any circumstance and providentially chooses which circumstances to actualise.
Galileo condemned (1633)
Galileo appeals to Augustine’s principle of accommodation; Rome condemns heliocentrism as contrary to Scripture. The affair later becomes the symbol of a supposed war of science and faith.
Lisbon earthquake shakes “best of all possible worlds” optimism
Leibniz had coined “theodicy” (1710); the Lisbon disaster and Voltaire’s satire made natural evil a central objection to providence.
Paley’s watchmaker: design in nature
William Paley’s Natural Theology argues from the contrivance of organisms to a designing Creator — the classic design argument Darwin read at Cambridge.
Gap theory harmonises Genesis with geology
Thomas Chalmers places geological ages between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2; later popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible.
Day-age and progressive creation
Hugh Miller and others read the days as ages corresponding to geological epochs; later held by William Jennings Bryan and Hugh Ross.
Darwin’s Origin of Species (1859)
Natural selection offers a non-teleological explanation of adaptation, undercutting Paley’s argument and raising new questions about suffering in nature.
Hodge: Darwinism as the denial of design
Charles Hodge objects not to an old earth but to Darwin’s exclusion of purpose; his Princeton successor B. B. Warfield would accept a providentially guided evolution.
Evolutionary creation: evolution as God’s method
Asa Gray’s Darwiniana and later Aubrey Moore, James Orr, Warfield, Teilhard and Dobzhansky see evolution as the providential means of creation.
Framework interpretation of the days
Arie Noordtzij (1924) and Meredith Kline (1958) read Genesis 1 as a literary structure of two triads crowned by the Sabbath.
Scopes trial (1925)
The prosecution of a Tennessee teacher for teaching evolution becomes a public humiliation for fundamentalism and drives creationism out of mainstream institutions.
Process theology: God persuades rather than controls
Whitehead and his followers reject both ex nihilo creation and coercive omnipotence: God lures the world and suffers with it.
The Holocaust and the crisis of theodicy
The murder of six million Jews in Christian Europe challenges every theodicy and the Church’s own record.
Humani Generis (1950) opens Catholic space for evolution
Pius XII permits study of the body’s evolution while requiring immediate creation of souls and rejecting polygenism; John Paul II (1996) calls evolution “more than a hypothesis”.
Young-earth creationism revived (The Genesis Flood)
Whitcomb and Morris recast Adventist flood geology for evangelicals, rejecting gap and day-age compromises.
Protest theodicy after Auschwitz
John K. Roth and others argue that justifying God before such evil is obscene; faith protests, laments and resists.
Free-will defence and skeptical theism
Plantinga’s free-will defence (1974) answers the logical problem of evil; Wykstra’s skeptical theism (1984) questions inferences from unseen reasons.
Open theism: God takes risks
Pinnock and colleagues argue that God does not exhaustively foreknow free choices; providence is responsive and relational.
Intelligent design movement
Johnson, Behe and Dembski revive the design argument at the molecular level.
Kitzmiller v. Dover (2005)
A federal court rules that ID is not science and cannot be taught in U.S. public-school science classes.
Today: a plural landscape

Catholic, Orthodox and mainline churches generally accept evolution under providence; many evangelicals, Pentecostals and Global South Christians hold young- or old-earth creationism, and creationist organisations are active from Korea and Brazil to Nigeria. Theodicy debates continue between Augustinian, Irenaean, skeptical, open and protest approaches; BioLogos, Answers in Genesis and Reasons to Believe embody three rival evangelical options.
